q: Pictured: footing. Which vernacular term names it?
ref: Know-How Architecture, “Building Technology: Construction Vernacular Terms” (#InstaFlashCards): term and image.
n: “Fundacion” is the vernacular for footing. Origin: Spanish fundación, the same root as English “foundation” (Latin fundare, to found).

q: Pictured: horizontal stud. Which vernacular term names it?
ref: Know-How Architecture, “Building Technology: Construction Vernacular Terms” (#InstaFlashCards): term and image.
n: “Pabalagbag / Trabe Anzo” is the vernacular for horizontal stud. Origin: trabe is Spanish for a beam, from Latin trabs. A horizontal stud is a small beam laid across the wall frame.

q: Pictured: rafter. Which vernacular term names it?
ref: Know-How Architecture, “Building Technology: Construction Vernacular Terms” (#InstaFlashCards): term and image.
n: “Kilo” is the vernacular for rafter. Native term; origin not confirmed. Kilo is used for both the truss and the rafter. Memory hook: think of the whole roof frame as kilo.

q: Pictured: reinforcing bars. Which vernacular term names it?
ref: Know-How Architecture, “Building Technology: Construction Vernacular Terms” (#InstaFlashCards): term and image.
n: “Kabilya” is the vernacular for reinforcing bars. Origin: Spanish cabilla “iron rod”, the usual word for rebar in Spanish.

q: Pictured: wall post. Which vernacular term names it?
ref: Know-How Architecture, “Building Technology: Construction Vernacular Terms” (#InstaFlashCards): term and image.
n: “Bagad” is the vernacular for wall post. Native Filipino term; origin not confirmed. Memory hook: bagad sounds like bakod “fence, enclosure”: the wall post is what a wall stands on.

q: Pictured: girder. Which vernacular term names it?
ref: Know-How Architecture, “Building Technology: Construction Vernacular Terms” (#InstaFlashCards): term and image.
n: “Guililian / Sepo / Kuling” is the vernacular for girder. Native/common terms for the main horizontal member of a house frame; origins not confirmed (Sepo may come from Spanish cepo “block, log”). Memory hook: guililian ~ gilid “side, edge”: the girder runs along the edges where beams rest.

q: Pictured: bottom chord. Which vernacular term names it?
ref: Know-How Architecture, “Building Technology: Construction Vernacular Terms” (#InstaFlashCards): term and image.
n: “Barakilan, Tirante” is the vernacular for bottom chord. Origin: tirante is Spanish for a tie, from tirar “to pull”. The bottom chord of a truss works in tension, pulling the two sides together.

q: Pictured: beam. Which vernacular term names it?
ref: Know-How Architecture, “Building Technology: Construction Vernacular Terms” (#InstaFlashCards): term and image.
n: “Biga” is the vernacular for beam. Origin: Spanish viga “beam”. Filipino spelling swaps v for b.

q: Pictured: ceiling joist. Which vernacular term names it?
ref: Know-How Architecture, “Building Technology: Construction Vernacular Terms” (#InstaFlashCards): term and image.
n: “Kostilyahe” is the vernacular for ceiling joist. Origin: Spanish costilla “rib” (costillaje = ribbing). Ceiling joists are the closely spaced ribs of the ceiling.

q: Pictured: truss. Which vernacular term names it?
ref: Know-How Architecture, “Building Technology: Construction Vernacular Terms” (#InstaFlashCards): term and image.
n: “Kilo” is the vernacular for truss. Native term; origin not confirmed. Kilo is used for both the truss and the rafter. Memory hook: think of the whole roof frame as kilo.
